key_terms.meaning: The single top of the Linux file tree; every other path starts here and there are no drive letters.
The on-disk record that holds a file's type, owner, group, mode, size, timestamps and data-block pointers, but not its name.
One of regular file, directory, block device, character device, FIFO, socket or symbolic link; the first character of ls -l shows it.
A directory where a separate filesystem is attached, so its contents appear inside the one tree.
Lists directory entries; with -l it also shows type, mode, links, owner, group, size and time.
Copies file contents to standard output in one go, with no paging; good for short files.
A pager that shows one screen at a time and can move both forward and backward without loading the whole file.
A simple pager that moves forward only, one screen at a time.
Copies file contents into a new inode, so source and copy are independent afterwards.
Renames or relocates a directory entry; inside one filesystem the inode itself does not change.
Removes a directory entry; the inode and its data are freed only when the link count reaches 0 and no process holds the file open.
Creates a hard link (a second name for the same inode) or a symbolic link (a new inode holding a path string).
Walks a directory tree and applies a test expression to each entry, then acts on the matches.
The ten characters printed by ls -l: one type character plus rwx triples for user, group and other.
Three digits, each from 0 to 7, where read = 4, write = 2 and execute = 1 are added per class.
Changes the mode bits, either symbolically (u+x, g-w, o=r) or with an octal number (644, 755).
A mask of bits removed from the default creation mode 666 for files and 777 for directories.
The single user whose numeric uid is stored in the inode; the first class in every permission check.
The numeric gid stored in the inode; a user matches it through the primary group or any supplementary group.
Change the owner and the group stored in the inode; only root may give a file to another user.

takeaways: All of Linux is one tree under /, and devices, pipes and sockets sit in that tree as files, so the same open, read and write calls work on them.
A name is not the file: the directory entry points to an inode, and the inode holds everything the kernel needs except the name.
cat is for short files, less is for long files because it reads lazily and pages both ways, more is the older forward-only pager.
cp creates new data, mv usually only rewrites a name, and rm deletes a name — which is why a hard link keeps data alive after the original name is gone.
The ten characters of ls -l are one type character plus three triples; the same information fits in three octal digits.
umask decides the mode of every new file and directory, so a wrong umask breaks group work silently.
The kernel checks root first, then owner, then group, then other, and stops at the first match, so a group permission never rescues the owner.
Root bypasses permission checks on ordinary files, which is convenient for repair and dangerous for accidents.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to describe the directory tree and file types, then read an ls -l line, compute a mode from an octal number or a umask, and explain link counts and the owner-group-other check order.

bank.q: Describe the Linux file system as a single tree under /. Name the purpose of /bin, /etc, /home, /var, /dev and /proc, and explain what a mount point is.
outline: One hierarchy, no drive letters
/ is the top; paths are absolute or relative
/bin and /usr/bin hold executables; /etc holds configuration text
/home holds user home directories; /var holds changing data such as logs
/dev holds device nodes; /proc is a virtual filesystem showing kernel state
A mount point is an existing directory where another filesystem is attached

bank.q: List the file types available in Linux. How does ls -l show the type, and why does Linux treat devices as files?
outline: Regular file (-), directory (d), block device (b), character device (c), FIFO (p), socket (s), symbolic link (l)
First character of the ls -l line gives the type
Devices as files let the same open/read/write/close calls work on hardware
/dev/tty and /dev/sda examples

bank.q: Explain the inode. List the fields it stores and state clearly what it does not store.
outline: Inode = index node, one per file, fixed number per filesystem
Fields: type, mode, link count, uid, gid, size, timestamps (atime, mtime, ctime), data block pointers
Does not store the file name; names live in directory entries
ls -i shows the inode number
Link count is the number of directory entries pointing at it

bank.q: Compare cat, more and less for viewing files, and say when each is the right choice.
outline: cat writes the whole file to standard output; no paging; use for short files or with | to pipe
more shows a screen at a time and only moves forward
less pages both ways, searches with /, does not read the whole file at start
less is preferred for long files and logs

bank.q: Draw the ten-character permission string produced by ls -l and explain each character with one example line.
outline: Character 1 = file type; characters 2-4 user, 5-7 group, 8-10 other
r = read, w = write, x = execute or enter directory, - = absent
Example: -rw-r--r-- means owner read/write, group read, other read
Directory x means the right to traverse; directory r means the right to list names

bank.q: Write the commands to create the tree project/src and project/doc, copy all .c files from src into doc, then rename doc to docs. State the effect on inodes.
outline: mkdir -p project/src project/doc
cp project/src/*.c project/doc/ creates new inodes with copied contents
mv project/doc project/docs is a rename; the directory inode is unchanged inside one filesystem
Absolute versus relative paths
Use of -i or -r where the command needs it

bank.q: A file shows -rw-r----- 1 ravi devs 4096 .. Give the symbolic and the octal command to make it rwxr-x---, and state exactly which users gain which rights.
outline: Current octal mode is 640
Target mode rwxr-x--- is 750
chmod u+x,g+x file and chmod 750 file are equivalent
Owner gains execute; group gains read and execute
Other still gets nothing

bank.q: With umask set to 027, what modes do touch notes.txt and mkdir work produce? Show the arithmetic and say whether a group member can edit notes.txt.
outline: Files start from 666; directories from 777
666 AND NOT 027 gives 640
777 AND NOT 027 gives 750
Notes.txt is rw-r----- so group can read but not write
Root's umask is often 022; set per login in the shell profile

bank.q: Use find to locate regular files larger than 1 MB under /home that were modified in the last 7 days, and then to delete empty directories under /tmp. Give both commands and explain each test.
outline: find /home -type f -size +1M -mtime -7
-type f selects regular files; -size +1M is larger than 1 mebibyte; -mtime -7 means modified less than 7 days ago
find /tmp -type d -empty -delete
Quote patterns; use -print or -exec where an action is needed

bank.q: Create a hard link and a symbolic link to a file, delete the original, and explain what each link now shows.
outline: ln data.txt hard.txt makes a second name for the same inode; link count becomes 2
ln -s data.txt soft.txt makes a new inode whose data is the path string
After rm data.txt the hard link still opens the data; the data is freed only at link count 0
The symbolic link breaks: it points to a name that no longer exists (dangling link)
Hard links cannot cross filesystems and cannot point to directories

bank.q: A user deletes a 5 GB log file with rm but df still shows the disk full. Explain why, and how to recover the space.
outline: rm removes the directory entry and lowers the link count to 0
A running process still holds the file open, so the inode and data blocks survive
The kernel frees blocks only when link count is 0 and no open file description remains
Find the process with lsof or /proc entries; restart or truncate it
Alternative: truncate the file with : > file or use > file before deleting

bank.q: Explain the order in which the kernel checks permissions. Use an example where the owner is denied but the group would have allowed the action.
outline: Root is checked first and normally bypasses the check (execute still needs at least one x bit)
Then owner if the file uid equals the process euid
Then group if the file gid matches the process egid or any supplementary group
Then other
Checks stop at the first match, so a mode of rw----r-- denies the owner nothing extra from other
Consequence: to give the owner a right, grant it in the user triple, not in other

bank.q: The rwx model gives only one owner and one group per file. Evaluate its limits for a shared project directory used by two teams, and describe how setgid on the directory helps.
outline: Only three classes exist, so per-user exceptions are impossible without ACLs
setgid on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group
Group write plus a umask of 002 lets a team share files
Sticky bit on a shared directory stops users deleting each other's files
ACLs (setfacl, getfacl) give per-user entries when the model is not enough
Trade-off: simplicity and speed of the basic check versus flexibility

bank.q: Compare cp, mv and ln as ways of making file data available at a second place. Judge which one saves disk space and which one is safest when the original is deleted.
outline: cp duplicates data into a new inode; independent, costs space
mv within one filesystem only renames the entry; no new data; across filesystems it copies then deletes
Hard link shares the inode; no extra space; safe against deleting the original name
Symbolic link holds a path; cheap but breaks if the target name disappears
Choice depends on disk budget, backup policy and whether the files must diverge later

glossary.def: A path that starts at / and names a location from the root of the tree.
A path interpreted from the current working directory rather than from /.
The identifier of an inode inside one filesystem, shown by ls -i and used by tools such as find -inum.
The number of directory entries that point at one inode; the data is freed when it falls to zero.
A second directory entry for an existing inode, created with ln and confined to one filesystem.
A file whose data is a path to another file, created with ln -s, allowed across filesystems.
A symbolic link whose target path no longer exists.
A file in /dev that represents a piece of hardware, block or character, identified by major and minor numbers.
A named pipe, a file type that carries a byte stream between processes and shows as p in ls -l.
A file type used as an endpoint for local interprocess communication, shown as s in ls -l.
A filesystem with no disk storage that presents kernel data as files, such as /proc and /sys.
The directory a process resolves relative paths against, printed by pwd and changed by cd.
The nine permission bits plus the special setuid, setgid and sticky bits stored in the inode.
The user id the kernel actually uses for permission checks, normally the same as the real uid.
Extra groups a user belongs to beyond the primary group; all of them count in the group check.
A mode bit that makes a program run with the file owner's effective uid, used by tools such as passwd.
On a program it runs with the file's group; on a directory it makes new files inherit that directory's group.
On a shared directory it stops users from deleting files they do not own, as in /tmp.
The process attribute whose set bits are cleared from the default creation mode of new files and directories.
The account with uid 0, which bypasses ordinary permission checks.
A program such as less or more that shows output one screen at a time and waits for a key press.
The default stream, file descriptor 1, that a command writes to, usually the terminal.
The shell's replacement of patterns such as *.c with matching names before the command runs.
